Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:19: And in the Gemara (Berachot 24b), chapter "Mi SheMeto": Rav Huna said, a Torah scholar is forbidden to stand in a filthy place, for he cannot be without Torah [in his thoughts]. And Rabbi Yochanan said, one may have [halachic] thoughts anywhere except in the bathhouse and the privy. It was taught: a person should not walk through filthy alleys and place his hand over his mouth and recite the Shema; and not only that, but if he was reciting and [a filthy alley] came upon him, he must stop - and if he did not stop, what [is his sin]? Rabbi Miyasha, grandson of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, said: of him Scripture says (Ezekiel 20:25), "and I also gave them statutes that were not good," and so on. Rav Adda bar Matna said: (Numbers 15:31), "because he has despised the word of the LORD and broken His commandment." Rav said: (Isaiah 5:18), "woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of falsehood." And if he did stop, what [is his reward]? Rabbi Abahu said: of him Scripture says (Deuteronomy 32:47), "and through this matter you shall prolong your days" - to this point. And Rashi explains, on Rav's statement "woe to those who draw iniquity": meaning, the way of most people in the world is that they commit transgressions for their own benefit, but this one commits a transgression for nothing - for he thinks he is performing a commandment by reciting [the Shema there], yet he commits a transgression by demeaning the Torah through that recitation; therefore, "woe to those who draw iniquity" for nothing - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:20: And in the Sefer Chasidim (section 949) they wrote that in the privy a person should think about his household expenses and what he needs; and Rabbeinu Yonah wrote in Sefer HaYirah that he should accustom himself to [such] calculations there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:21: Further, one must be careful about the honor of the [divine] Name, that the Name of Heaven not be profaned through him - as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Yoma 86a), in these words: our Rabbis taught, when a person recites [Scripture] and studies [Mishnah] and attends upon Torah scholars, and his speech is gentle with people, and his business dealings in the marketplace are pleasant, and he conducts his transactions faithfully, what do people say about him? Happy is so-and-so who studied Torah, happy is his father, happy is his teacher who taught him Torah; woe to people who did not study Torah - so-and-so who studied Torah, see how pleasant his ways are, how proper his deeds! Of him Scripture says (Isaiah 49:3), "and He said to me, you are My servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified." But when a person recites and studies, and his speech is not gentle with people, and his business dealings in the marketplace are not pleasant, and he does not conduct his transactions faithfully, what do people say about him? Woe to so-and-so who studied Torah, woe to his father and his teacher who taught him Torah; happy are people who did not study Torah - so-and-so who studied Torah, see how ugly his deeds are, how corrupt his ways! Of him Scripture says (Ezekiel 36:20), "in that it was said of them, these are the people of the LORD, yet they have gone out of His land."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:22: And further it says there: what constitutes a chillul Hashem [profanation of the divine Name]? Rav said: such as myself, if I take meat from the butcher and do not pay for it immediately. Rabbi Yochanan said: such as myself, if I walk four cubits without [thinking of] Torah or without tefillin. Rav Nachman bar Rabbi Yitzchak said: such as when people say, may his Master forgive so-and-so. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi said: such as when his colleagues are ashamed of a teaching reported in his name - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:23: And it is already known how strict our Rabbis, of blessed memory, were concerning chillul Hashem; it says there: but one who is guilty of chillul Hashem - repentance has no power to hold his sin in suspension, nor does Yom Kippur have power to atone for it, nor do sufferings have power to scour it away, but all of these hold it in suspension, and death alone scours it away, as it is said (Isaiah 22:14), "surely this iniquity shall not be atoned for you until you die, says the LORD of hosts" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:24: And in the Zohar (Pinchas 231a) it says that the first to be judged on Rosh Hashanah is one who is not careful about the honor of the LORD, as it is said (Job 1:6), "and the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD"; in these words: the first judgment of all - who is it? One who does not honor the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, and does not honor the Torah and its servants; likewise, who does not take care that the holy Name not be profaned on earth - to this point. And they said, of blessed memory (Vayikra Rabbah 22:6): we find that the Holy One, blessed be He, overlooked idolatry but did not overlook chillul Hashem, as it is said (Ezekiel 20:39), "and you, O house of Israel, thus says the LORD God: go, serve every one his idols... but My holy Name you shall no longer profane" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:25: And concerning the matter of chillul Hashem, I have seen fit to copy the words of the pious Rabbi Yosef Yavetz, peace be upon him, on the Mishnah (Avot 4:4), "whoever profanes the Name of Heaven in secret" - and the end of the Mishnah's text is, "is punished for it in public, whether it was unwitting or deliberate, in the matter of chillul Hashem." And Rabbi Yehudah ibn Shoshan explains: "whether unwitting or deliberate" is a distinct reason in itself - just as secret and public are equal in [the severity of] chillul Hashem, so are the unwitting and the deliberate. And the reason is: one who transgresses the King's command - there is a difference between transgressing in secret or in public; but one who raises a hand against the king himself - it is all the same, and if we came to judge, it would be fitting to punish the secret one more than the public one, for one who raises a hand against the king among his nobles and officers - his own foolishness will save him [as an excuse], but in secret he has no merit at all. And so too the matter of unwitting versus deliberate: for every person is obligated to write on the tablet of his heart that there is a King who rules over everything, and that it is fitting to fear Him and tremble at His honor - and one who transgresses this, his blood is on his own head. Could a person say to a king, I forgot and struck you, I forgot and cursed you? - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:26: And the aforementioned pious author further wrote that included within "chillul Hashem in secret" is one who speaks evil-speech about his fellow in secret - for he thereby transgresses [in severity comparable to] idolatry, sexual immorality, and bloodshed, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said, that evil speech is greater than all of them. And the proof of this is the matter of Miriam, who spoke evil speech in secret and unwittingly, and yet was punished for it in public - "and the people did not journey until Miriam was gathered in" - as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained, so that everyone would know the punishment for evil speech - to this point, summarizing his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:27: The second distinction concerning the matter of honor is what is written concerning the sons of Eli (I Samuel 2:29), "why do you kick at My sacrifice and My offering," and so on, "and honor your sons above Me, to make yourselves fat with the choicest of all the offerings of Israel My people." It appears that one must be careful not to honor any man or woman before honoring the Holy One, blessed be He - similar to what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 14a), that it is forbidden to greet one's fellow before praying, [as it says of] one who comes early to his door [without having prayed yet]; and therefore the Torah commanded that the first of everything be given to the priest, who is the portion of the LORD - whether concerning the challah offering, which is called "reishit" [first], or concerning the terumah offerings, and likewise the bikkurim [first fruits].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:28: Further, the second distinction, "and honor your sons above Me" - one must be careful not to honor any person such that his honor exceeds the honor of the Omnipresent - as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Kiddushin 33b) concerning a certain student who sat before his teacher: Rabbi Abahu said, a Torah scholar is permitted to stand before his teacher only [twice daily], morning and evening, so that his honor not exceed the honor of Heaven - to this point. And Maimonides, peace be upon him (Laws of Torah Study 6:8), ruled the halachah according to Rabbi Abahu; and although the Rosh and Rav Alfasi hold that the halachah does not follow Rabbi Abahu, since the honor of a Torah scholar is equal to the honor of the Omnipresent - "the LORD your God shall you fear" including Torah scholars - nevertheless, the practical difference applies to other people, that it is not fitting to stand before them or honor them more than the honor of the Omnipresent.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:29: Further, there is another distinction encompassing all the commandments, which is to honor the Omnipresent as one honors people whom he is obligated to honor, such as kings and dignitaries - and this is what is meant by "and honor your sons above Me" - meaning, would that we were equal, but instead you have honored them more than Me! And this is along the lines of what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 28b): let the fear of Heaven be upon you like the fear of flesh and blood - so too, let the honor of Heaven be upon you like the honor of flesh and blood. And this is the middling measure; but it is proper to honor the Holy One, blessed be He, more than people, along the lines of "honor the LORD with your wealth" (Proverbs 3:9), which Rabbeinu Yonah, peace be upon him, explains as "more than your wealth" (see Sefer Chasidim, section 275) - for it is known that a king of flesh and blood, were he to command some commandment, how carefully would one perform it with heart and soul for the honor of the king; correspondingly, one should honor his Creator. And Chovot HaLevavot elaborated on this distinction in the Gate of Self-Reckoning, the tenth consideration; see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:30: And they said, of blessed memory, in Midrash Shmuel (chapter 12), concerning the matter of the Ark that was in the camp of the Philistines for six months, that the Holy One, blessed be He, was displeased with Israel over this; in these words: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak said, the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: if one of you had lost his rooster, would he not have searched several alleys until he found it? But My Ark wanders in the field of the Philistines and you are not concerned about it! [Nevertheless] "His own right hand and His holy arm brought Him salvation" - to this point. And this is what is explained, that one must be careful of the honor of the Omnipresent like the honor of flesh and blood.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:31: Further, one branch grows from this: to be careful of the honor of one's soul more than the honor of one's body. And we find that the soul is called "kavod" [glory/honor] - for since the soul is a portion of Him, blessed be He, one who honors it through Torah and the observance of commandments and good deeds honors the Holy One, blessed be He; whereas the body, created from a putrid drop, is a portion of this world, a portion of mankind, and the body ultimately decays and is lost - just as all the good things of this world will eventually return to loss and destruction, because they are drawn from the serpent's skin and its husk. It follows that one who honors his body more than his soul is like one who honors people more than the Holy One, blessed be He; therefore he should be careful to honor his soul more than the honor of his body, and should not give the "first" to his body, but should first repair the honor of his soul, and afterward his body - as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 10b), that it is forbidden to eat before praying; and in the Zohar (Beshalach 62b) it likewise says that before eating one must occupy himself with Torah, as it is said (Proverbs 13:25), "the righteous eats to the satisfaction of his soul" - after his soul is satisfied with Torah and prayer. And this is what is meant by "to make yourselves fat with the choicest of all," and so on, as explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:32: And similarly for all matters, one should not put his own affairs before the affairs of Heaven. For example, if he is a craftsman, he should divide the day, half for his craft and half for occupying himself with Torah, so that the honor of his body be equal to the honor of his soul; and before engaging in his craft he should occupy himself with Torah, to give the "first" to his soul, in such a way that the Torah is primary and the craft secondary - and by this merit he will succeed in his craft, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Avodah Zarah 19b), "this matter is written in the Torah," and so on, that one who occupies himself with Torah, his possessions succeed - on condition that he put Torah before his craft, as I explained. And so the verses prove: (Psalms 1:2), "but his delight is in the Torah of the LORD," and so on, and afterward, "and whatever he does shall prosper" - and other verses likewise prove this. But if he puts his own affairs before the affairs of Heaven, he will come to neglect Torah, as it says (Avot 4:10), "if you neglect the Torah, you will have many things causing you to neglect it" - and this matter has been tested among many.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:33: And so too, from all the matters of the world by which a person honors himself, one should take proof to honor his soul - and this is what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said in the Midrash (Yalkut Mishlei, remez 932), on the verse (Proverbs 2:4), "if you seek her as silver" - in these words: Scripture teaches that just as a person is careful with his coin [sela] not to lose it, so he must be careful with his learning not to lose it. And just as silver is hard to acquire, so words of Torah are hard to acquire. Or perhaps, just as silver is hard to lose, so too are words of Torah? The verse teaches (Job 28:17), "gold and glass cannot equal it" - hard to acquire like gold, but easy to lose like a glass vessel - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:34: And along these lines they said there, on this verse: Reish Lakish said, if a person does not go after words of Torah, they will not come after him. And so (Avot 4:14), Rabbi Nehorai says, exile yourself to a place of Torah. And if a person searches after them, through this he merits wisdom and understanding, as it is said (Proverbs 2:5), "and you shall find the knowledge of God" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:35: It follows that just as a person honors his body by pursuing silver and gold - and if he were told, go to such-and-such a place and there you will earn so much money, he would not cease striving with diligence and alacrity - so should he strive with diligence and alacrity after the honor of Torah, which is the honor of his soul, for there is no honor in the World to Come except Torah, as it is said (ibid. 3:35), "the wise shall inherit honor."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:36: And so too, just as he honors his body with fine garments, he should adorn his soul with beautiful commandments - a beautiful tallit, beautiful tefillin - as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (on Exodus 15:2), "this is my God, and I will glorify Him" - beautify yourself before Him in the commandments. In tractate Shabbat, chapter "Rabbi Eliezer of Milah" (133b): "this is my God, and I will glorify Him" - beautify yourself before Him in the commandments: make a beautiful sukkah, a beautiful lulav, a beautiful shofar; write a Torah scroll for His name's sake, with fine ink, with a fine quill, by a skilled scribe, and wrap it in fine silks. Abba Shaul says: be like Him - just as He is merciful and gracious, so you too be merciful and gracious - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:37: Further, there is another distinction close to what we have written, which is what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Shabbat 113a), that Rabbi Yochanan would call his garments "my honorers" [mechabdotai]. And from this we may extend the analogy to the matter of the soul - for just as this body is honored among people when its garments are fine and without stain and the like, so the soul is honored in the World to Come only through its garment, which is the limbs of the body, when they are made fine through the fulfillment of the commandments, and likewise fine without the stains of sin and without any blemish - through this, honor is drawn to the soul; but if one of these is lacking, there is no honor for the soul. And to this they alluded in the Tikkunim (22b), saying "fine garments upon its limbs" - for just as a person needs fine garments to clothe himself, so his limbs, which are the garment of his soul, need to be fine, under the conditions I explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:38: The third distinction: that one not regard himself highly in a place where there is the honor of the LORD - and the proof of this is the matter of David, when Michal, daughter of Saul, rebuked him, saying to him (II Samuel 6:20), "how the king of Israel honored himself today, uncovering himself today before the eyes of the maidservants of his servants, as one of the vulgar fellows shamelessly uncovers himself!" And King David, peace be upon him, answered (ibid. 6:22), "and I will be yet more vile than this, and will be lowly in my own eyes," and so on. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said in the Sifrei, in these words: she said to him, my father's house was more dignified than yours - Heaven forbid that a mere palm or sole or heel was ever seen uncovered among them; rather, all of them were more dignified than you. And in Midrash Rabbah, Parashat Bamidbar (4:20), it says: they were modest and holy. And what did David say? "Before the LORD, who chose me," and so on - your father's house sought their own honor and abandoned the honor of Heaven, but I do not do so; rather, I set aside my own honor and seek the honor of Heaven - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:39: And behold, Michal, daughter of Saul, rebuked King David, peace be upon him, appropriately according to reason - namely, that it is not fitting for the honor of the LORD that one demean himself by leaping and whirling, for he will necessarily expose himself, and the honor of the LORD requires that a person conduct himself with gravity. And David answered her that since the honor of the LORD cannot be less than this [full devotion], I set aside my own honor and seek the honor of Heaven - meaning, he seeks that the honor of Heaven be visible to all; and had he walked with gravity, the honor of Heaven would not have been visible to all.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:40: And we thus learn a fourth distinction concerning the matter of the honor of the LORD: that sometimes one must be careful of the honor of the LORD by being of grave demeanor - such as while standing in prayer and the like - and this is the explanation of the word "kavod" [honor], from the term "kaveidut" [heaviness/gravity]; and the proof is "and the vile shall be [set] against the honorable [nichbad]" [an implied contrast].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:41: But when it is a time of joy, to gladden the Omnipresent, the honor of the LORD consists precisely in demeaning oneself by leaping and whirling - and along these lines we find Aaron the priest, whom the LORD commanded (Leviticus 6:3), "and he shall take up the ashes," despite all his greatness; and likewise Elazar son of Aaron, of whom it is said (Numbers 4:16), "and the appointment of Elazar son of Aaron the priest is the oil for the light, and the incense of spices, and the daily grain-offering, and the anointing oil."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:42: And in Midrash Rabbah (Bamidbar Rabbah 4:20), commenting on this verse, our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said: "and the appointment of Elazar son of Aaron the priest," and so on - this is [the meaning of] (Proverbs 25:6), "do not glorify yourself before the king, and do not stand in the place of the great." If before a king of flesh and blood a person must conduct himself with lowliness, how much more so before the Omnipresent! And we have learned: be bold as a leopard, light as an eagle, swift as a deer, and mighty as a lion, to do the will of your Father in Heaven - to teach you that there is no room for pride before the Omnipresent. Elijah says: whoever increases the honor of Heaven and diminishes his own honor, the honor of Heaven increases and his own honor increases; and whoever diminishes the honor of Heaven and increases his own honor - the honor of Heaven remains in its place, but his own honor is diminished. There was an incident with a certain man, and so on - two incidents are brought there [in the Midrash], and we have already copied the discourse of Tanna Devei Eliyahu that brought these incidents, in the Gate of Fear, chapter 4.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:43: And it says there in Midrash Rabbah, after the aforementioned incidents: from here you learn that a person should not conduct himself with pride before the Omnipresent, for whoever exalts himself before Him is demeaned; and so it says (I Samuel 2:30), "for those who honor Me I will honor, and those who despise Me shall be lightly esteemed." And so you find with David, king of Israel, that he did not conduct himself with pride before the Omnipresent, but demeaned himself before Him like a commoner, in order to increase the honor of the Omnipresent. When was this? At the time he brought up the Ark from the house of Avinadav, which was in Giv'ah, to bring it to Jerusalem - this is (II Samuel 6:1), "and David again gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand." David said: I will not bring up the Ark quietly. Immediately he took counsel with the officers of the thousands and hundreds, that they should send throughout the whole Land of Israel for people to gather to them and go to bring it up, as it is said (I Chronicles 13:1), "and David took counsel with the officers of thousands and hundreds, with every leader," and so on. And they said further there (II Samuel 6:4), "and Achio walked before the Ark" - from here they said, "his brother walked before it." Once they brought it up, ninety thousand elders were walking before it, and the priests carried it, and the Levites played music, and all Israel rejoiced - one with a lulav in his hand, another with a drum and musical instruments in his hand - this is (ibid. 6:5), "and David and all the house of Israel played before the LORD," and so on - this refers to the lulav that a person waves.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:44: And further, there, just below (ibid. 6:14), "and David whirled with all his might before the LORD" - come and see how much David demeaned himself for the honor of the Holy One, blessed be He: David should have simply walked before it as a king, dressed in his royal garments - not so; rather, he dressed in fine garments for the honor of the Ark and rejoiced before it, insofar as it can be said, as it is said (I Chronicles 15:27), "and David was clothed in a robe of fine linen, as were all the Levites who bore the Ark," and so on, for it is written, "and David whirled with all his might before the LORD" - what is "with all his might"? With all his strength. What is "whirled" [mecharker]? That he was clapping his hands together and stamping and saying, "keiri ram" [a musical exclamation], while Israel shouted and blew trumpets and all kinds of musical instruments, as it is said (II Samuel 6:15), "and David and all Israel brought up the Ark of the LORD," and so on. Once Israel came to Jerusalem, all the women were peering at David from the roofs and windows and saw him dancing and playing, and he did not care - this is "and it came to pass, as the Ark of the LORD came into the city of David," and so on - behold, this shows his own wife looking down at him from a window; and from where do we know that all the women of Jerusalem did so? Because she says to him, "how the king of Israel honored himself today, uncovering himself today before the eyes of the maidservants of his servants" - "and Michal saw King David leaping and whirling," and so on - once she saw him making himself like a commoner, he became demeaned in her eyes.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:45: And they further elaborate there on what she said, "as one of the vulgar fellows shamelessly uncovers himself" - they explain there that this means "the most vulgar of the vulgar," meaning that there is no one more devoid than he of [regard for] all the commandments. And he answered, "and I will be yet more vile than this" - and it says there: and do not say that I was so [only] in the eyes of others and not in my own eyes - the verse teaches, "and I will be lowly in my own eyes; but with the maidservants of whom you spoke, I will gain honor." He said to her: those daughters of Israel, whom you called maidservants, are not [mere] maidservants but [true] mothers - would that I have a portion with them in the future to come! This is "but with the maidservants of whom you spoke - would that I gain honor with them." And because Michal spoke thus, she was punished, for it is written afterward (ibid. 6:23), "and Michal the daughter of Saul had no child until the day of her death"; but is it not written (II Samuel 3:5), "and the fifth, Yitream, by Eglah, David's wife" - meaning that she cried out like a heifer [eglah] and died? This is why it is written "until the day of her death" - implying that on the day of her death she did have [a child, but died in childbirth].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:46: There is no one in Israel who demeaned himself for the sake of the commandments more than David - for behold, he said before the LORD (Psalms 131:2 [131:1-2]), "O God, my heart was not haughty" - at the time Samuel anointed me king; "nor were my eyes raised up" - at the time I killed Goliath; "and I did not occupy myself with great matters" - at the time they restored me to the kingship; "or with things too wonderful for me" - at the time I brought up the Ark - "surely I have stilled and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with his mother" - just as an infant is not ashamed to expose himself before his mother, so I stilled my soul before You, that I was not ashamed to demean myself before You for Your honor - "like a weaned child with me is my soul" - like this infant who comes forth from his mother's womb and has no haughty spirit about nursing from his mother's breast, so was my soul upon me, that I am not ashamed to learn Torah even from the youngest of Israel. Rabbi Ada bar Chinena said: the Holy One, blessed be He, said to him, you compared yourself to a weaned child - by your life, just as this infant has no sins, so you have no sins, as it is said (II Samuel 12:13), "the LORD also has removed your sin; you shall not die." From here you learn that a person is not permitted to conduct himself with pride before the Omnipresent, but rather must demean himself for His honor.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:47: Rabbi Yehuda HaLevi bar Shalom said: the deeds of the Holy One, blessed be He, are not like the deeds of flesh and blood. Why? A servant of a flesh-and-blood master has fine garments; when he goes out to the marketplace he wears them, but when he stands to cook, he removes the fine ones and puts on torn and worn-out ones; and further, when he sweeps out the stove and the oven, he wears even worse ones than those. But before the Holy One, blessed be He, at the time a priest sweeps out the altar and removes its ashes, he would wear the finest garments, as it is said (Leviticus 6:3), "and the priest shall put on his linen garment," and so on, for the purpose of "and he shall take up the ashes" - why so? Rather, to make known that there is no pride before the Omnipresent. And so you find with Elazar, who conducted himself with lowliness before the Omnipresent. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: Elazar was a chief over chiefs and a prince over princes, as it is said (Numbers 3:32), "and Elazar son of Aaron the priest shall be chief over the chiefs of the Levites," and so on - see what authority was in his hands! And you might think that, since he was a great man, he would give it to others to carry the vessels that he was supposed to carry - not so; he himself would carry them, as it is said (ibid. 4:16), "and the appointment of Elazar son of Aaron the priest," and so on. And where did he carry all these? Our Rabbis said, this is how he would carry them: the oil for the light in his right hand, the incense of spices in his left hand, and the daily grain-offering hanging from his arm; and the anointing oil, where was it? Rabbi Acha said in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai: the flask was shaped like a lentil, and he would put it inside his belt - because he was girded at his loins with his implements, like a servant before his Master - to make known that there is no haughtiness before God. "The appointment of the whole Tabernacle and all that is in it, in holiness and its vessels" - through him they were given the Ark, the table, the menorah, and the altars and all their vessels, as it is written, "and your charge shall be the Ark," and so on, "and Elazar son of Aaron shall be chief over the chiefs of the Levites," and so on - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:48: And in the Yerushalmi (Shabbat 10:3), they say: one oil vessel in his right hand, one oil vessel in his left hand, the incense in his bosom, and the wafers on his shoulder - behold, according to his greatness was his lowliness, to carry all this burden at once for the honor of the Omnipresent.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:49: And they said (Keritot 28b) that a certain priest performed the [Temple] service wearing silk gloves on his hands, whereas the law is that nothing should interpose between his hands and the service - and his punishment was that his hands were cut off by order of the [Roman] government.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:50: And of this category of honor is to honor the synagogue and the study hall - for since the synagogue is a place where the Shechinah, called "kavod," rests, as King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 26:8), "I love the habitation of Your house, and the place where Your glory dwells" - and so too Isaiah the prophet said concerning the matter of the Temple (Isaiah 60:13), "to beautify the place of My sanctuary, and I will make the place of My feet glorious" - and it is known that a synagogue is called "a small sanctuary," as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained in Megillah, chapter 3 (29a). Therefore one must honor it and sweep it and remove from it all dust and dirt and the like, in the way one honors the houses of kings; and it is said in the Sefer Chasidim (section 128) concerning Rashi's grandfather, that he would sweep the place of the ark that held the Torah scroll with his beard.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:51: Further, concerning the matter of the synagogue: it is proper to be careful, when leaving the synagogue, not to leave with one's back to the Heichal [ark] holding the Torah scroll, but rather to keep his face turned toward the ark; and likewise when descending from the platform where the Torah scroll rests. And this is learned from the sons of Kehat, who did this when they carried the Ark - in these words, in the Midrash (Bamidbar Rabbah 5:8): and in another respect they were superior to all the Levites - for those who carried [other parts of] the whole Tabernacle would walk in the normal manner, with their faces toward the direction they were walking, but the sons of Kehat would walk backward, with their faces toward the Ark, so as not to turn their backs on the Ark. Behold, this teaches you that although they were greater than the other families - and needless to say than [ordinary] Israel - their spirit was not haughty on account of this, but rather they were subservient before the Ark. Why so? Because there is no greatness before God - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:52: Further, concerning the honor of the synagogue: one should not spit in it if possible; and if it is not possible, being naturally prone to it, he should spit discreetly under his garments and rub it away with his feet - and on Shabbat he should cover it with his feet and not rub it, unless it is a stone floor. And best of all is to have a special cloth to wipe his spittle, so as not to bring the spittle out of his mouth into the air of the synagogue - and thereby he will escape the reckoning of judgment that they mentioned, that one who spits before his fellow and it is repulsive is punished, as explained in the Gemara (Chagigah 5a), which we copied above. And it is also the way of kings that none of their officers spits in their courtyard, and certainly not in their house - and the general rule for matters of fear is: let the fear of Heaven be upon you like the fear of flesh and blood.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:53: Further, concerning the honor of the synagogue: one should not raise his voice in it to call any person or the like, for it is the way of those who sit in the king's house not to raise their voice before him, but to speak in a hushed voice. And behold, the testament of the Ramban, peace be upon him, to his son, that he conduct himself with the way of humility and never raise his voice, except in Torah and prayer - because "the whole earth is full of His glory" - and this is part of the practice of humility, and it is fitting to uphold it always, and certainly all the more so while standing in the house of the King, the King of the world, where His Shechinah dwells, that it is fitting to conduct oneself with this humility; and by this he shows that he has fear of the Shechinah and fulfills the commandment, "and you shall fear My sanctuary."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:54: And the reason that reverence is obligatory for a sanctuary and holy places is because every place that has holiness requires fear, as we explained above - for concerning this Jacob our father, peace be upon him, said (Genesis 28:17), "and he was afraid, and said, how awesome is this place! This is none other than the house of God." And Onkelos translated it, "this is no ordinary place," and so on - and this is because it is the way of those who sit before a king that his awesomeness is upon them; and although His glory, blessed be He, fills the world, out of His love for us He contracted His Shechinah among us, just as He would contract His Shechinah between the staves of the Ark and in the Holy of Holies. And so too regarding the Tent of Meeting, we find that after it was completed it is written (Exodus 40:35), "and Moses was not able to enter the Tent of Meeting, because the cloud rested upon it, and the glory of the LORD filled the Tabernacle." And so too in the Temple, when Solomon brought the Ark into the Holy of Holies, it is written there (I Kings 8:11), "and the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD" - and so too the synagogue is filled with the light of the glory of the LORD, and although we do not see anything, we must believe this with complete faith.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:55: And it is fitting that we make a kal vachomer [a fortiori argument] to honor the synagogue from the honor we give elders - for the honor of elders, as we wrote above, is "for who sees the supernal, holy beard," and so on, "who is not put to shame by it" - and correspondingly, who would see the preciousness of the Shechinah, called kavod, and not be put to shame? And if you say that it is not visible, then you are lacking in faith - and along these lines it says in Parashat Va'etchanan (260b), that one who opens his eyes while reciting the Amidah prayer demeans the Shechinah, having no fear of the Shechinah - and from this we learn for the other holy things in the synagogue. And we will elaborate further on the matter of the synagogue in the Gate of Holiness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:56: And just as a person is obligated to conduct himself with honor in the synagogue because of its holiness, so it is fitting to conduct oneself with holiness in the study hall, for the law is that the holiness of the study hall exceeds the holiness of the synagogue. And so it is fitting to conduct oneself with honor toward the mezuzah, because of the honor of the holiness of the [divine] Name within it; and it is explained in the Zohar (Va'etchanan 264a) that one should be careful not to pour dirty water in front of the mezuzah, in these words: and therefore a person must not make filth and dirt at the doorway, and must not pour out murky water - one reason, so as not to show disrespect toward the Name of his Master; and the other, because the Destroyer has permission to destroy [there] - and therefore a person should be careful of this, and a person should be careful not to withhold the Name of his Master from the doorway of his house - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:57: And one who refrains from honoring the Omnipresent for the sake of the honor of this world is punished; and of him Isaiah the prophet said (Isaiah 10:3), "and what will you do on the day of visitation, and in the desolation that shall come from afar? To whom will you flee for help, and where will you leave your glory?" And so it says in the "Margenita" of Rabbi Meir, as we copied above.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Fear 15:58: There is yet another distinction concerning the matter of honor, which is to distance oneself from the honor of this world - for the more a person honors himself, the more the supernal honor flees from him, as it is said (Proverbs 12:9), "better is one lightly esteemed who has a servant," and so on - and this will be further elaborated in the Gate of Humility.
